notes.meaning: Azariah began to reign over Judah during the reign of Jeroboam II of Israel. He is also known by the name Uzziah in other scriptures. His coming to power marked the start of a long period of renewed strength and stability for Judah.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic scholars note that the name Azariah in Kings may reflect an early copyist variation for Uzziah, who is listed in the family line of Jesus in Matthew 1:8–9.

notes.meaning: Azariah was only sixteen years old when his rule began, and he remained on the throne for fifty-two years. A reign of this length gave the southern kingdom remarkable peace and prosperity. The biblical record honors him by naming his mother, Jecoliah of Jerusalem.

Azariah followed the true God, doing what was right just as his father Amaziah had done early in his life. God blessed his kingdom with victory, wealth, and great building projects while he sought the Lord. Even good leaders need continuous humility to finish well.

Even during this prosperous reign, the outdoor pagan shrines called high places were left standing. The people continued to offer sacrifices and burn incense at these local altars instead of at the temple in Jerusalem. While the king accomplished much good, he failed to remove this compromise in worship.

The Lord struck King Azariah with leprosy, a serious skin disease, so he had to live in a separate house for the rest of his life. Second Chronicles explains that this happened because pride led him to enter the temple and unlawfully burn incense like a priest. His son Jotham took charge of the palace and governed the daily affairs of the land.

The other events of Azariah's life, including his military triumphs and extensive building projects, were preserved in the royal records of Judah. Second Chronicles supplies many of these details that Kings passes over. The biblical authors recorded only what was needed to show God's hand in his reign.

Azariah died and was buried near the tombs of the kings in the City of David. Because he was a leper, he was laid to rest in an adjoining burial field rather than inside the royal tombs. His faithful son Jotham then succeeded him as the sole king of Judah.

In the north, Zechariah became king of Israel in Samaria, but he ruled for only six months. His brief time on the throne followed a period of confusion and strife after his father Jeroboam died. His quick downfall showed the growing instability of the northern kingdom.

Zechariah walked in the evil ways of his ancestors rather than turning to the Lord. He kept the golden calf worship that Jeroboam son of Nebat had set up generations earlier to keep the northern tribes away from Jerusalem. Israel's kings continually repeated these old sins instead of seeking God.

A conspirator named Shallum assassinated Zechariah openly in front of the people and took the throne. The public nature of the murder showed how unpopular Zechariah had become and how lawless the nation was. This violent act brought a sudden end to the royal house of Jehu.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that ancient Greek translators misread the Hebrew phrase for 'in front of the people' as a proper name, leading to older guesses that a conspirator named Keblaam or Zobolam was involved.

notes.meaning: The rest of Zechariah's short reign was set down in the official chronicles of Israel's kings. Even though he governed for only six months, the royal scribes kept a record of the events and the unrest of his day. Every leader's deeds, whether long or short, stand remembered before God.

Zechariah's death fulfilled the exact promise God gave to King Jehu four generations earlier. The Lord had declared that Jehu's descendants would sit on Israel's throne down to the fourth generation, but no further. God faithfully keeps every word He speaks, both His promises and His warnings.

Shallum took power in Judah's thirty-ninth year of Uzziah, but his rule lasted only one single month. Power gained through treachery and bloodshed proved impossible to hold. His sudden fall showed how quickly ungodly ambition can collapse.

Menahem marched an army from Tirzah to Samaria, killed Shallum, and seized the crown for himself. Menahem was likely a military commander who refused to accept Shallum's violent takeover. Israel had descended into brutal power struggles where military might decided who ruled.

The remaining events of Shallum's one-month reign and the story of his plot were noted in the royal annals of Israel. His violent overthrow showed the tragic pattern of northern politics. Rebellion against God's ways brought endless division and sudden ruin.

Menahem brutally attacked the town of Tiphsah and its surrounding region because the citizens refused to open their gates to him. To terrify anyone who might oppose him, he committed terrible atrocities, even ripping open pregnant women. Such horrific violence showed how deeply the northern kingdom had fallen away from God's moral law.

Menahem established himself on Israel's throne during Azariah's thirty-ninth year and managed to rule for ten years. Unlike several of the kings around him, he was able to keep power long enough to pass it to his son. Yet his decade of rule was marked by terror and heavy burdens on the people.

Throughout his decade on the throne, Menahem lived wickedly in the sight of the Lord. He never turned away from the golden calf worship begun by Jeroboam son of Nebat. Despite all his military strength, he completely failed to lead the nation spiritually.

King Pul of Assyria invaded Israel, and Menahem paid him a massive tribute of one thousand talents of silver. Menahem gave this fortune so the Assyrian empire would prop him up and secure his hold on the throne. Instead of crying out to God for protection, Israel's king turned to a brutal pagan superpower for help.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Assyrian records confirm that Pul was the Babylonian throne name of Tiglath-pileser III, whose royal inscriptions specifically record receiving tribute from Menahem of Samaria.

notes.meaning: To raise the enormous tribute, Menahem forced every wealthy man in Israel to pay fifty shekels of silver. This heavy tax allowed him to pay off the invaders, and the Assyrian army withdrew from the land for a time. Buying temporary peace with money only advertised Israel's weakness and invited future invasions.

The other actions of Menahem and what he achieved during his reign were written in the official records of Israel. Those ancient documents recorded the political maneuvers of his ten years on the throne. Scripture focuses mainly on how he stood in relationship to God.

Menahem died a natural death and was buried, leaving the crown to his son Pekahiah. In an era when most northern kings were murdered, Menahem was one of the few who died in bed. Yet leaving a kingdom founded on blood and heavy taxes provided no lasting peace for his family.

Pekahiah son of Menahem began ruling over Israel in Samaria during the fiftieth year of Azariah of Judah. His reign lasted only two years before violence caught up with his family line. The political ground in the northern kingdom remained fragile and full of danger.

Pekahiah continued the ungodly ways of his father and clung to the calf worship started by Jeroboam. He showed no desire to reform the nation or guide the people back to the true God. Spiritual stubbornness kept leading Israel down a path toward national disaster.

Pekah son of Remaliah, a high-ranking military officer, conspired against Pekahiah and assassinated him inside the palace citadel in Samaria. Pekah carried out the murder with the aid of fifty men from Gilead. The very soldiers trusted to guard the king turned against him to seize power for themselves.

The other deeds of Pekahiah during his two-year reign were recorded in the royal history books of Israel. Even a brief and failed reign did not escape the record keepers of the day. God sees and measures the impact of every leader, whether their time is short or long.

Pekah son of Remaliah became king in Samaria during the fifty-second and final year of Azariah's reign in Judah. He managed to hold onto the throne for twenty years. Though he gained the kingdom by treason, his long rule showed his forceful political and military grip.

Pekah did evil in the Lord's sight, refusing to turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had brought upon Israel. Like those before him, he supported false worship to keep his kingdom separate from Jerusalem. Worldly shrewdness without godliness only leads a nation deeper into ruin.

During Pekah's reign, King Tiglath-pileser of Assyria swept in and captured major northern and eastern territories of Israel, including Gilead and Galilee. The invaders carried many of the people away into exile in Assyria. This was the first major deportation of Israel, showing that the northern kingdom was crumbling under God's judgment.

Hoshea son of Elah formed a conspiracy, assassinated Pekah, and took the throne for himself. This overthrow happened in the twentieth year after Jotham had begun his rule in Judah. Pekah died by the same violent treason he had once used against his own master.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars explain the dating to Jotham's twentieth year by counting from the start of his co-regency with Uzziah, which places Pekah's death in the early reign of Jotham's son Ahaz.

notes.meaning: The rest of Pekah's actions and accomplishments were recorded in the chronicles of the kings of Israel. Though Kings mentions his twenty-year reign in only a few verses, other scriptures show he had a huge impact through his wars against Judah. Earthly ambition and military alliances could not protect him from ultimate defeat.

In the south, Jotham son of Uzziah began to reign as king of Judah during Pekah's second year over Israel. Jotham had already helped run the government while his father lived in isolation with leprosy. Now he took over direct leadership of the Davidic dynasty.

Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began his sole reign, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother was Jerusha, the daughter of Zadok, likely from a prominent priestly family. Unlike the chaos in the north, Judah continued to enjoy an orderly family succession.

Jotham did what was right in the sight of the Lord, following the good pattern of his father Uzziah. Chronicles notes that he carefully avoided his father's arrogant mistake of entering the temple sanctuary to offer incense. He was one of Judah's most upright kings, serving God faithfully throughout his life.

Even under Jotham, the outdoor high places were not removed, and the people continued to sacrifice and burn incense there. Jotham did, however, show great devotion to true worship by rebuilding the Upper Gate of the Lord's temple. He repaired and honored God's house even though he could not persuade all his people to give up their local shrines.

The rest of Jotham's deeds and accomplishments were preserved in the royal records of Judah. Second Chronicles details how he defeated the Ammonites and built strong towers and defensive walls. His quiet, steady faithfulness brought real blessing and security to his land.

Toward the end of Jotham's days, the Lord began sending King Rezin of Aram and King Pekah of Israel to attack Judah. Although these foreign rulers acted out of their own political greed, Scripture shows that God was using them as a rod of discipline against Judah. Trouble was beginning to brew on Judah's borders to test the nation's faith.

Jotham died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, having lived an honorable and faithful life. His son Ahaz then took the throne in his place. A godly father unfortunately gave way to a son who would lead Judah into spiritual ruin.
